content: Has anyone ever thought about Grassmannians, and how to best include them in Lean/Physlib?
My lack of spelling means I missed this docs#Module.Grassmannian, though this is not particularly physics friendly I don't think (and I'm not even sure is the right thing).

Based on the module doc-string it looks like this is a more general definition more compatible with other mathematics and can recover the more standard definition you might be expecting, but that conversion is a todo item

Ok, actually I think docs#ExteriorAlgebra is much closer to what we need here.

I've never found a good reference on any of this stuff, and tbh find it very confusing. However, I think I managed to come to the following conclusions:

  1. The Tensor we have currently in Physlib is for bosonic contractions of indices, and does not take account of the grassmanian nature of the underlying fields.
  2. When we write down a term in a lagrangian we want the fields to be grassmanian valued.
  3. The lagrangian itself is also grassmanian valued.
  4. What "grassmanian valued" means here depends on the the underlying context, and specifically what dynamical fields one has at play.
  5. Take for example a theory with a single LeftHandedWeyl fermion. The dynamics can be described holomorphically in terms of the coordinates of LeftHandedWeyl x RightHandedWeyl. (We need RightHandedWeyl to account for the fact we want complex conjugates).
  6. Potentials (without derivatives) of this theory live in the ExteriorAlgebra ℂ (LeftHandedWeyl x RightHandedWeyl). This can be seen as associating a single grassmannian variable with every of the coordinates in LeftHandedWeyl x RightHandedWeyl. Each new dynamical fermionic field gives us a new set of varibles within this exterior algebra (via e.g. the exterior product).
  7. If we want to go further, and include derivatives, we need the ExteriorAlgebra of the jet fiber of the trivial bundle with fiber LeftHandedWeyl x RightHandedWeyl. It is this ExteriorAlgebra where the lagrangian actually lives.
  8. If one puts an ordering on the coordinates of LeftHandedWeyl x RightHandedWeyl, one can in theory map the lagragngian down to a complex number - although this is nevery actually done in physics.

Importantly it appears that extending our Tensor to cover this case is a research level question. However, it not actually necessary to do this to build up a large API of useful results.

I think a good test of all of this would be to:

  1. Give ExteriorAlgebra ℂ (LeftHandedWeyl x RightHandedWeyl) a suitable name (maybe LeftHandedWeyl.potentialAlgebra).
  2. Define on it the action of the Lorentz group (extending that on LeftHandedWeyl x RightHandedWeyl).
  3. Define the Majorana mass within this algebra.
  4. Show it is invariant under the Lorentz group.

(This is perhaps a good reference in this latter direction: https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/DermisekDiracField.pdf, also this)

What I don't understand here is that it seems that a potential has type:V : ExteriorAlgebra ℂ (LeftHandedWeyl x RightHandedWeyl). I don't understand how we evaluate V at a given value of the fermion (if this is even indeed possible). Or rather relates to sections of the spinor bundle.
My wild guess is that you want a Clifford algebra (where Grassmann’s theory lives), not an exterior algebra.
Will look into this more, though I think ExteriorAlgebra in Mathlib is just an abbreviation for a specific Clifford algebra (whether it is the right one is a different question).
This is what I have got here for the 'effective potential of a left-handed Weyl fermion: Physlib#1415
